 Guy Ritchie 's The Gentlemen is a terrific crime series. It has everything that makes the filmmaker's work so entertaining, from eccentric criminals and sharp dialogue to elaborate schemes and sudden bursts of violence. Theo James makes Eddie Horniman's transformation from reluctant aristocrat to criminal operator very enjoyable, while Kaya Scodelario gives Susie Glass enough confidence to steal almost every scene.

 The Netflix series stands out for finding humor in the collision between Britain's upper class and its underground weed empire. Still, Ritchie has another show that makes an even stronger case for his storytelling instincts. Released on Prime Video in 2026, Young Sherlock trades the criminal underworld for Victorian murder investigations, giving the director another famous British character to play with. And this time, Ritchie gets to dive into the origins of a literary legend.
 'Young Sherlock' Sends Baker Street's Great Detective Back to Oxford
 Close Prime Video 
 Prime Video 
 Paramount Pictures 
 Set in 1871, Prime Video's Young Sherlock follows a 19-year-old Sherlock Holmes (Hero Fiennes Tiffin) at Oxford University. He's hardly the polished consulting detective audiences recognize. Instead, he's reckless, frequently in trouble, and still figuring out what to do with his extraordinary intelligence.
 When a murder investigation makes Sherlock a prime suspect, he must clear his name while uncovering a conspiracy that reaches far beyond the university. Along the way, he meets James Moriarty (Dónal Finn), a fellow intellectual misfit who becomes his unlikely partner.
 The Prime Video series draws inspiration from Andrew Lane's Young Sherlock Holmes novels, but it doesn't adapt their plots directly. Lane's books follow Sherlock as a 14-year-old schoolboy, whereas showrunner Matthew Parkhill wanted an older protagonist whose experiences could lead toward the detective Sir Arthur Conan Doyle introduced in A Study in Scarlet .
 Parkhill also avoids retelling the original stories, using the space before that first novel to invent new experiences. It's a smart way to revisit Sherlock Holmes, considering he has inspired countless adaptations, from Basil Rathbone's classic movies to Benedict Cumberbatch's modern-day BBC detective.
 Young Sherlock's casting is particularly interesting . Hero Fiennes Tiffin, who once starred as young Tom Riddle in Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince , plays Holmes as a cheerful pickpocket with more bounce than recent screen interpretations. Dónal Finn, best known as Mat Cauthon in The Wheel of Time , gives Moriarty a roguish charm. The two share crackling chemistry throughout the show.

 Instead of introducing Moriarty as an obvious villain, Young Sherlock lets the two men enjoy each other's company. Knowing what their relationship eventually becomes adds an extra layer to every exchange. Natascha McElhone and Joseph Fiennes play Sherlock's parents; Max Irons and Zine Tseng's Princess Shou'an widen the circle; and Colin Firth pops up as Sir Bucephalus Hodge.
 'Young Sherlock' Has a More Compelling Mystery Than 'The Gentlemen'
 Theo James stars in The Gentlemen  Netflix  Prime Video 
 As entertaining as The Gentlemen is, the Netflix series plays it safe. It delivers another variation on themes Guy Ritchie has explored for decades, starting from movies like Snatch and Lock, Stock and Two Smoking Barrels . That's not necessarily a bad thing. Not every director understands criminal underworlds, shifting loyalties, and chaotic power struggles as well as he does. But if you're already familiar with Ritchie's best gangster thrillers or the original The Gentlemen , you know what you're getting.
 The Gentlemen is an entertaining gangster comedy, but its appeal comes largely from watching colorful characters scheme their way through one mess after another. Young Sherlock has a more defined mystery to solve, and the murder at Oxford gives its eight episodes a strong narrative backbone. It's a risky venture as it refuses to rely on established archetypes.
 Young Sherlock builds an entirely new television identity. The show blends detective fiction, coming-of-age storytelling, historical adventure, and action-thriller elements into a binge-worthy story . One episode might focus on a puzzling murder, and the next could dive into a larger conspiracy.
 Our verdict
 Watch this if
 You love clever mysteries with a little chaos.
 You enjoy seeing famous rivalries before they turn ugly.
 Skip this if
 You want Sherlock to be the finished genius.
 Victorian intrigue isn't your cup of tea.
 Will you watch this?
 Yes No Already seen 
 The structure also gives Ritchie a chance to explore a different kind of character evolution. Eddie Horniman learns to navigate a world he never wanted to join, but Sherlock is becoming someone who doesn't yet exist. The series cleverly uses that familiarity as an advantage. It explores his family relationships, his impulsiveness, and the experiences that could eventually turn him into a detached observer. Watching the world's greatest detective develop his methods and traits is intriguing in a way The Gentlemen isn't.
 That's not to say one show makes the other obsolete. The Gentlemen remains one of Netflix's strongest crime dramas, and Ritchie's fingerprints are all over the production. But Young Sherlock demonstrates something even more impressive. It proves that after all these years, Guy Ritchie can still surprise audiences.
